questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a concern about a "visible vein" in his right shoulder area. He reports that the vein becomes more pronounced during exercise or when lifting heavy objects. There is no associated pain, redness, or swelling. He denies any history of trauma to the area. On inspection of the right shoulder area reveals a prominent, non-pulsatile, linear structure running along the deltopectoral groove is seen. Which of the following structure is seen in this area?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cephalic vein

 

The structure described as a prominent, non-pulsatile, linear structure running along the deltopectoral groove is the cephalic vein. The cephalic vein is a visible superficial vein in the deltopectoral groove, the space between the deltoid and pectoralis major muscles. This vein becomes more prominent during activities such as exercise or lifting heavy objects due to increased blood flow. It is essential to note that there are no associated symptoms like pain, redness, or swelling, which confirms the prominence of the vein without any pathological process.

 

The deltopectoral groove is formed by the deltoid muscle laterally and the pectoralis major muscle medially. It is an important anatomical landmark for identifying the cephalic vein. This area also contains the clavipectoral fascia, which is pierced by four structures: one vein (cephalic vein), one artery (thoracoacromial artery), one nerve (lateral pectoral nerve), and one lymphatic vessel. This anatomical configuration explains the presence of the cephalic vein as a visible, non-pulsatile structure in the region.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Axillary artery: The axillary artery is located deeper in the axilla and is not visible superficially. Moreover, the axillary artery is a pulsatile structure, unlike the non-pulsatile cephalic vein described in this case.

 

Options C. Basilic vein: The basilic vein is located on the medial aspect of the arm and is not found in the deltopectoral groove. It is incorrect in this scenario because it does not course through the area described.

 

Options D. Radial nerve: The radial nerve runs posteriorly in the arm and does not pass through the deltopectoral groove. Therefore, it is not the structure seen in this area.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The cephalic vein is a visible superficial vein that runs along the deltopectoral groove and becomes more prominent during activities such as exercise or lifting heavy objects. It is a non-pulsatile structure, making it easily distinguishable from arteries in the region.

questions.stem: Who is often referred to as the "Father of modern Anatomy" due to his excellent works in the field of human anatomy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Vesalius

 

Vesalius is referred to as the Father of modern Anatomy. He was responsible for revitalizing the study of human anatomy through human dissection, which allowed for more accurate and detailed observations compared to earlier practices. Vesalius published "De Humani Corporis Fabrica" in 1543, which corrected many anatomical misconceptions held since the era of Galen, who had dissected animals rather than humans. Vesalius's works set the foundation for modern anatomical studies.

 

Hippocrates is regarded as the Father of Medicine, while Galen contributed significant knowledge in anatomy, but his era was marked by the dissection of animals, leading to many inaccuracies in human anatomy. This period is often referred to as the dark era of anatomy. The great cerebral vein is named after Galen. 

 

Herophilus is considered the Father of Anatomy, as he was the first to systematically study the human body, but his work predates Vesalius.

 

Educational objectives:

 

Andreas Vesalius is recognized as the Father of modern Anatomy for his groundbreaking work in human dissection and the publication of detailed, accurate anatomical observations in his book, which revolutionized the study of human anatomy.

questions.stem: In the anatomical arrangement of intermuscular spaces such as the cubital fossa, femoral triangle, anatomical snuff box, etc., what primarily forms the roof of these spaces? 1.Skin2.Superficial fascia3.Subcutaneous fat, cutaneous nerves and vessels4.Deep fascia
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 1, 2, 3, 4

 

The roof of anatomical spaces like the cubital fossa, femoral triangle, and anatomical snuff box is formed by multiple layers. These layers consist of skin, which is the most superficial layer, followed by superficial fascia, which contains subcutaneous fat, cutaneous nerves, and vessels, and deep fascia, which provides structural support and separates the muscles and deeper structures. These layers create a protective covering for the underlying anatomical structures in the mentioned spaces.

 

Each of these layers plays an important role in the structural integrity of these regions. The skin forms the outermost layer, the superficial fascia contains the fat and vessels that provide nourishment and insulation, and the deep fascia adds strength and provides a framework for deeper tissues like muscles and bones.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The roof of intermuscular spaces such as the cubital fossa, femoral triangle, and anatomical snuff box is formed by skin, superficial fascia, subcutaneous fat, cutaneous nerves and vessels, and deep fascia.

questions.stem: Hilton's Law of Anatomy is most closely associated with which principle?

options.label: A
options.text: The relationship between muscle innervation and joint function.

options.label: B
options.text: The correlation between blood supply and organ health.

options.label: C
options.text: The connection between the nerve supplying a joint and the muscles moving the joint.

options.label: D
options.text: The relationship between the size of a muscle and its strength.

questions.answerText: The connection between the nerve supplying a joint and the muscles moving the joint.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The connection between the nerve supplying a joint and the muscles moving the joint.

 

Hilton's Law states that the nerve supplying a joint also supplies the muscles that move the joint and the skin covering the muscles. This principle highlights the anatomical and functional connection between nerve innervation and joint movement. The same nerve that innervates the joint also controls the muscles responsible for moving the joint, creating a cohesive functional relationship between the nerve, muscle, and joint.

 

This principle is essential in understanding how the nervous system coordinates movement and sensation, ensuring that any injury or pathology in one area (e.g., the joint) may affect other connected structures, such as the muscles or skin.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. The relationship between muscle innervation and joint function: This option is close but incomplete, as it doesn't fully encompass the relationship between nerve innervation of the joint, muscles, and skin as described by Hilton's Law.

 

Options B. The correlation between blood supply and organ health: This is unrelated to Hilton's Law, which focuses on nerve supply rather than blood supply.

 

Options D. The relationship between the size of a muscle and its strength: This option is incorrect as it addresses muscle physiology and strength, which is not related to Hilton's Law.

 

Educational objectives:

 

Hilton's Law explains that the same nerve supplies both a joint, the muscles that move the joint, and the overlying skin, highlighting a functional relationship between these structures.

questions.stem: Concept of "Anatomical position" is very essential for all kinds of operative procedures and to understand and publish articles. About the anatomical position, which of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The palms of the hands are facing posteriorly.

options.label: C
options.text: The feet are dorsiflexed at the ankles.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) The thumbs are oriented laterally.

 

In the anatomical position, the body is standing erect, eyes looking forward, arms hanging by the sides with the palms facing forward (not posteriorly), and the thumbs are oriented laterally. The feet are together, with the toes pointing forward, and the elbows are fully extended (not flexed). This standard position is used to describe the relative positions of body parts in anatomy and is crucial for surgical procedures, medical documentation, and scholarly publications.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. The palms of the hands are facing posteriorly: This is incorrect as, in the anatomical position, the palms are facing forward.

 

Options C. The feet are dorsiflexed at the ankles: In the anatomical position, the feet are not dorsiflexed but are placed flat on the ground, with the toes pointing forward.

 

Options D. The elbows are fully flexed: The elbows are extended, not flexed, in the anatomical position.

 

Educational objectives:

 

In the anatomical position, the body is standing erect with palms facing forward, thumbs oriented laterally, elbows extended, and feet placed flat on the ground. This position is universally used for anatomical reference.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with anterior knee pain that worsens with activities like running and jumping. On physical examination, there is tenderness and swelling over the front of the knee. Palpation reveals a small, round, bony prominence at the center of the knee. The patient reports no recent trauma. You will put the involved bone in which of the following types?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Sesamoid

 

The bone involved here is the patella, the largest sesamoid bone in the body. Sesamoid bones are seed-like bones embedded within tendons and function to reduce friction, modify pressure, and protect tendons from stress. In this case, the patella is located in the knee, within the quadriceps tendon. The patient’s anterior knee pain, which worsens with running and jumping, is related to the stress on the patella during these activities.

 

Sesamoid bones are peculiar because they lack periosteum, Haversian canals, and medullary cavities. These bones are formed after birth,

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Sphenoid: The sphenoid bone is located in the skull and is unrelated to the knee, making this option incorrect.

 

Options B. Hyoid: The hyoid bone is found in the neck, not in the knee, and thus is irrelevant to this case.

 

Options C. Ethmoid: The ethmoid bone is part of the skull, specifically the nasal region, and has no connection to the knee.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the body. Sesamoid bones are seed-like bones that lack periosteum, Haversian canals, and medullary cavities. They are essential for reducing friction in tendons and protecting them from stress, particularly during activities such as running and jumping.

No periosteum

 

No Haversian canals

 

No medullary cavity

questions.stem: Where is the growth plate of cartilage in a long bone located?

options.label: B
options.text: Between the diaphysis and the epiphysis

questions.answerText: Between the diaphysis and the epiphysis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Between the diaphysis and the epiphysis

 

The growth plate of cartilage in a long bone, also known as the epiphyseal plate, is located between the diaphysis and the epiphysis. This is the area where the lengthening of the bone occurs during growth. The bone grows in length as new cartilage cells are produced, which then ossify (turn into bone tissue) over time. This process continues until skeletal maturity, after which the growth plate becomes ossified and is replaced by bone, ceasing further growth in length.

 

 

The long bone consists of three main parts:

 

  1. Diaphysis – the shaft of the bone.
  2. Epiphysis – the ends of the bone.
  3. Metaphysis – the flared part of the diaphysis near the growth plate.

 

The metaphysis is the region where the diaphysis meets the epiphysis, and the growth plate is found here, allowing the bone to lengthen during childhood and adolescence.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. In the diaphysis: The diaphysis is the shaft of the long bone, not the location of the growth plate.

 

Options C. In the epiphysis: While the epiphysis forms the ends of the bone, the growth plate is located between the epiphysis and diaphysis, not within the epiphysis itself.

 

Options D. In the medullary canal: The medullary canal is the central cavity of the bone where bone marrow is stored, and it has no direct involvement with the growth plate.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The growth plate or epiphyseal plate is located between the diaphysis and the epiphysis of a long bone, and this region is responsible for the bone's lengthening during growth.

questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old patient, Suyash, came to the OPD with a history of a fall on his hand. He is now experiencing pain in the hand region. The X-ray of the patient is given. Which of the following joint has been shown in his X-ray?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ellipsoid joint

 

In the provided X-ray, the joint displayed is the radiocarpal joint (wrist joint), which is an ellipsoid joint. This joint is located between the radius and the proximal carpal bones (mainly the scaphoid and lunate).

 

Ellipsoid joints are characterized by their oval-shaped articular surfaces, which allow movement in two planes—flexion/extension and abduction/adduction. This structure is ideal for the wrist, enabling a wide range of motion but limiting rotational movements, which are instead handled by the distal radioulnar joint.

 

Key points from the X-ray:

 

  • The radius can be seen articulating with the scaphoid and lunate bones of the wrist.
  • This type of joint is classically referred to as an ellipsoid joint because of its shape and movement.

 

Mnemonic for Carpal Bones:

 

 

"Shyam Lal Tinde Pakao Tumhare Tinde Kacche Hai"

 

  • Scaphoid
  • Lunate
  • Triquetrum
  • Pisiform
  • Trapezium
  • Trapezoid
  • Capitate
  • Hamate

 

The radiocarpal joint allows ellipsoid joint movements like flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction, but not rotation. Therefore, it fits the criteria of an ellipsoid joint.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Hinge joint: Hinge joints, like the elbow, permit movement in only one plane (flexion and extension). This type of joint is not seen in the wrist.

 

Options B. Ball-and-socket joint: These joints, such as the shoulder and hip, allow movement in multiple planes (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation). The wrist joint, however, does not fit this description.

 

Options D. Saddle joint: The saddle joint is found at the first carpometacarpal joint (thumb), where the first metacarpal and trapezium articulate, allowing for a greater range of motion. This joint is not visible in the provided X-ray.

questions.stem: Which type of joint allows for rotational movement of the forearm, specifically allowing pronation and supination?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pivot joint

 

The pivot joint allows for rotational movement of the forearm, specifically pronation and supination.

 

Supination means the superior facing of the palm.

 

Pronation means the downward facing of the palm.
These are rotatory movements, and wherever there is rotation, the joint involved is the pivot joint.

 

Other Options: 

 

Options A. Hinge joint: The hinge joint is found at "SHIT."
Remember the mnemonic:

 

S for Shoulder joint (ball and socket joint)

 

H for Hip joint (ball and socket joint)

 

I for Incudomalleolar joint (in the ear)

 

T for Talocalcaneonavicular joint (ball and socket joint)

 

The hinge joint is not involved in rotation.
Examples of hinge joints include:

 

I for Interphalangeal joints

 

E for Elbow joint

 

A for Ankle joint (all are uniaxial)

 

Options B. Ball-and-socket joint: This type of joint is found in the shoulder and hip and allows for multi-axial movement, but it's not responsible for the rotation of the forearm.

 

Options D. Saddle joint: The saddle joint has an S-shaped articulating surface.
Examples include the patellofemoral joint and the first carpometacarpal joint (base of the thumb).
These joints are not responsible for rotational movement like pronation and supination.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The pivot joint allows for rotational movement of the forearm, specifically pronation and supination.

questions.stem: Which two joints are responsible for the nodding and shaking movements of the head, respectively?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Atlanto-axial joint and atlanto-occipital joint

 

The nodding ("yes") movement of the head occurs at the atlanto-occipital joint, which is the joint between the atlas (C1) and the occipital bone of the skull. This joint allows for flexion and extension, creating the nodding motion. It is an ellipsoid joint (or condylar joint, as some texts describe it).

 

The shaking ("no") movement of the head occurs at the atlanto-axial joint, which is the joint between the atlas (C1) and the axis (C2). This joint allows for rotation, which enables the side-to-side shaking movement of the head. The atlanto-axial joint is a pivot joint, where the odontoid process (dens) of the axis serves as the pivot around which the atlas rotates.

 

Important Points:

 

The atlanto-occipital joint is responsible for the yes movement (nodding).

 

The atlanto-axial joint is responsible for the no movement (shaking).

 

The C1 (atlas) sits above the C2 (axis), and the odontoid process (dens) of the axis is crucial for the rotation movement.

 

Other Options:

 

Options B. Sternoclavicular joint and costovertebral joint: These joints are involved in the movement of the clavicle and ribs, respectively, but have no role in head movement.

 

Options C. Sacroiliac joint and hip joint: These joints are involved in the movement of the lower body and pelvis, not the head.

 

Options D. Glenohumeral joint and temporomandibular joint: The glenohumeral joint is the shoulder joint, and the temporomandibular joint is located in the jaw. Neither of these joints is responsible for head movements like nodding or shaking.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The atlanto-occipital joint (between C1 and the occipital bone) allows for the nodding movement ("yes").

 

The atlanto-axial joint (between C1 and C2) allows for the shaking movement ("no"), as it is a pivot joint allowing for rotational movement.

questions.stem: What is the typical fiber arrangement of lumbrical muscles in the hand?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1st & 2nd lumbricals – Unipennate, 3rd & 4th lumbricals - bipennate

 

The lumbrical muscles are small intrinsic muscles of the hand responsible for the flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at the interphalangeal joints. This positioning is often described as the pen-holding position or the Babaji kathulu position.

 

The 1st and 2nd lumbricals have a unipennate fiber arrangement. These muscles are located on the lateral side of the hand and are innervated by the median nerve.

 

The 3rd and 4th lumbricals have a bipennate fiber arrangement. These are on the medial side of the hand and are supplied by the ulnar nerve.

 

Additional Information:

 

Damage to the median nerve affects the 1st and 2nd lumbricals, while damage to the ulnar nerve affects the 3rd and 4th lumbricals. This is significant in clinical conditions like claw hand:

 

Complete claw hand occurs when both the median and ulnar nerves are affected.

 

Partial claw hand occurs when only the ulnar nerve is affected, causing the 3rd and 4th lumbricals to be paralyzed while the 1st and 2nd lumbricals remain functional.

 

Educational objectives:

 

1st and 2nd lumbricals: Unipennate, innervated by the median nerve.

 

3rd and 4th lumbricals: Bipennate, innervated by the ulnar nerve.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after falling onto her outstretched hand. She complains of severe pain in her elbow. Physical examination reveals swelling and tenderness over the distal humerus. An X-ray confirms a supracondylar fracture. Upon further examination, the patient is unable to flex her thumb. Which nerve is most likely involved in this patient's presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anterior interosseous nerve

 

In cases of supracondylar fracture, the most commonly involved nerve is the median nerve. The median nerve gives off a deep branch called the anterior interosseous nerve, which supplies the deep muscles in the anterior compartment of the forearm. These include:

 

Flexor pollicis longus (responsible for thumb flexion),

 

Flexor digitorum profundus (lateral half), and

 

Pronator quadratus.

 

Since the flexor pollicis longus is innervated by the anterior interosseous nerve, damage to this nerve causes difficulty with thumb flexion—explaining why the patient is unable to flex her thumb.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Deep branch of ulnar nerve: This nerve is not involved in thumb flexion or the injury described.

 

Options B. Posterior interosseous nerve: This nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm and is not involved in thumb flexion.

 

Options D. Superficial branch of ulnar nerve: This nerve is responsible for sensory innervation and does not affect thumb flexion.

questions.stem: A surgeon is performing a dissection in the shoulder region and notes the structures passing through the clavipectoral fascia. Which of the following structures is known to pierce the clavipectoral fascia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Thoracoacromial Artery

 

The clavipectoral fascia is pierced by several important structures. 

 

Among the options, the thoracoacromial artery is the correct answer. It pierces the clavipectoral fascia and supplies blood to the pectoral and shoulder regions.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Axillary Nerve: The axillary nerve passes posteriorly through the quadrangular space, not through the clavipectoral fascia.

 

Options C. Suprascapular Artery: This artery passes over the scapula and does not pierce the clavipectoral fascia.

 

Options D. Long Thoracic Nerve: The long thoracic nerve runs on the lateral aspect of the thoracic wall and is not associated with the clavipectoral fascia.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The thoracoacromial artery is one of the main structures that pierce the clavipectoral fascia.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements is wrong about the nerve involved in causing the deformity in the given image?

options.label: A
options.text: It passes deep to the flexor retinaculum

options.label: B
options.text: In the lower half of forearm it has a subfascial course

options.label: C
options.text: It enters the palm on the ulnar side of the pisiform bone

options.label: D
options.text: It rests on the flexor carpi ulnaris

questions.answerText: It passes deep to the flexor retinaculum
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) It passes deep to the flexor retinaculum

 

The deformity shown in the image is ulnar claw hand, which results from damage to the ulnar nerve. This injury causes clawing of the fourth and fifth fingers due to unopposed flexion at the interphalangeal joints and extension at the metacarpophalangeal joints.

 

Regarding the course of the ulnar nerve:

 

It does not pass deep to the flexor retinaculum. Instead, it passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon’s canal. The statement that the ulnar nerve passes deep to the flexor retinaculum is therefore incorrect.

 

In the lower half of the forearm, the ulnar nerve runs subfascially.

 

The ulnar nerve enters the palm on the ulnar side of the pisiform bone, which is correct.

 

The ulnar nerve rests on the flexor carpi ulnaris as it runs along the forearm, another correct statement.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The ulnar nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon’s canal and is involved in causing the deformity known as ulnar claw hand. The incorrect statement in this case is that it passes deep to the flexor retinaculum.

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old patient presents to the orthopedic clinic with complaints of progressive weakness in his right hand. The patient reports difficulty in fine movements of the hand. The doctor performed a test over the patient, as shown in the image. Which of the following statements is true about the given image?

options.label: A
options.text: The median nerve of the right hand is injured.

options.label: B
options.text: There is weakness of thenar muscles on the right side.

options.label: C
options.text: The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak.

options.label: D
options.text: The flexor muscles of the thumb of the right hand are weak.

questions.answerText: The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The adductor pollicis of the right side is weak

 

The test shown in the image is called the Froment's sign, also known as the book test. This test is used to assess the function of the ulnar nerve, specifically the function of the adductor pollicis muscle. In the normal hand, the patient should be able to hold a book (or paper) using adduction of the thumb. The ulnar nerve is responsible for this movement through the adductor pollicis muscle.

 

In this patient, the ulnar nerve is damaged, leading to weakness of the adductor pollicis muscle. As a result, the patient compensates by using the flexor pollicis longus (supplied by the median nerve) to flex the thumb while holding the paper, as seen in the image. This is why the thumb flexes rather than adducts.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. The median nerve of the right hand is injured: This is incorrect because the median nerve is not responsible for the adduction of the thumb. It innervates the flexor pollicis longus, which is compensating in this test.

 

Options B. There is weakness of the thenar muscles on the right side: This is incorrect because the thenar muscles (which are innervated by the median nerve) are not affected. The issue is with the adductor pollicis (innervated by the ulnar nerve).

 

Options D. The flexor muscles of the thumb of the right hand are weak: This is incorrect because the flexor muscles of the thumb (innervated by the median nerve) are functioning and are compensating for the weakened adductor pollicis.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The Froment’s sign is a test for ulnar nerve damage, specifically testing the adductor pollicis muscle. When the ulnar nerve is damaged, the patient compensates by using the flexor pollicis longus, resulting in flexion of the thumb instead of adduction.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old female presented to the medicine OPD with complaints of numbness over her little finger of the right hand. On examination, there was total loss of cutaneous sensation over the palmar and dorsal surface of the little finger of the right hand. Which of the following nerves is probably injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ulnar nerve

 

The key clue here is the numbness over the little finger of the right hand, with a total loss of cutaneous sensation over both the palmar and dorsal surfaces of the little finger. This sensory loss indicates that the ulnar nerve is involved because the little finger is located on the ulnar side of the hand.

 

The ulnar nerve is responsible for supplying sensation to the medial one and a half fingers: the little finger and half of the ring finger. In this case, the entire little finger, both palmar and dorsal surfaces, is affected, confirming the involvement of the ulnar nerve.

 

It’s important to remember the dermatomes of the hand:

 

The radial nerve supplies the base of the thumb and part of the hand on the dorsal side but does not innervate the little finger.

 

The median nerve supplies the first three fingers and half of the ring finger on both the palmar and dorsal aspects.

 

The ulnar nerve supplies the remaining part of the hand, specifically the little finger and half of the ring finger, including both the palmar and dorsal surfaces.

 

Thus, the ulnar nerve is the nerve that would be responsible for the complete sensory loss described in the little finger.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The ulnar nerve supplies both the palmar and dorsal surfaces of the little finger, and damage to this nerve results in a total loss of sensation in this area.

questions.stemHtml: An eight-year-old male child managed to take his board game from the loft after standing on top of two chairs one over the other. But while trying to get down, he fell from the topmost and experienced severe pain over his right hand, back, and leg. The image given is his X-ray. options.label: A

The image shows the hand of an 8-year-old child, and it is important to recognize that the carpal bones have a specific timeline for ossification. At this age, not all of the carpal bones may be fully ossified, and this is why some might not be visible on the X-ray. Specifically, the pisiform bone is not seen in this X-ray, which is expected because the pisiform bone ossifies later, typically around 12 years of age. 

 

Other Options:

Options D. Lunate is the smallest carpal bone: This is also incorrect. The pisiform is the smallest carpal bone, not the lunate. The pisiform is a sesamoid bone and is the smallest of the carpal bones.

The pisiform bone is the last carpal bone to ossify, typically around 12 years of age, and is not visible in X-rays of younger children, as seen in this 8-year-old patient's case.

The structure labeled A in the image is the pectoralis minor muscle. This muscle originates from the 3rd, 4th, and 5th ribs near their costal cartilages and inserts into the coracoid process of the scapula.

 

When the pectoralis minor muscle contracts, it pulls the coracoid process forward, resulting in the protraction of the scapula, not retraction. Therefore, the statement that the pectoralis minor muscle retracts the scapula is incorrect. Retraction refers to pulling the scapula backward, a movement typically performed by muscles like the trapezius and rhomboids, not the pectoralis minor.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old obese man felt a snap in his right lower leg while playing squash and couldn’t continue the game further. He reached the emergency department with complaints of acute severe pain in his right lower leg and heel. The physician confirmed a diagnosis of an acute right Achilles tendon rupture and the patient was immediately posted for open reparative surgery. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: It is the strongest tendon of the human body

options.label: D
options.text: It inserts into the upper third of the calcaneus

questions.answerText: It is the strongest tendon of the human body
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It is the strongest tendon of the human body

 

The Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in the human body, known for its durability and ability to withstand the immense force generated during activities like running and jumping. In this patient’s case, a snap in the Achilles tendon caused severe pain, a common presentation for an acute rupture of this tendon.

 

  1. Dorsiflexion of the foot at the ankle joint is incorrect. The Achilles tendon is responsible for plantar flexion of the foot, not dorsiflexion. Plantar flexion involves the downward movement of the foot, such as pressing down on a gas pedal.
  2. The Achilles tendon is not supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve. The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment muscles, including the muscles that form the Achilles tendon (gastrocnemius and soleus).
  3. Insertion of the Achilles tendon is not into the upper third of the calcaneus. It inserts into the calcaneal tuberosity, a bony prominence on the back of the heel bone (calcaneus).
  4. The correct statement is that the Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon of the human body, as it withstands significant stress during activities such as running and jumping.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in the human body and is involved in plantar flexion of the foot. It is supplied by the tibial nerve and inserts into the calcaneal tuberosity.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lateral compartment of leg


The patient sustained a fracture of the lower fibula. Following this injury, she developed pain and numbness over the dorsum of her left foot, along with difficulty turning her sole outwards. This outward movement is called eversion, and eversion is performed by the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles, which are located in the lateral compartment of the leg. The common peroneal nerve is responsible for innervating these muscles. Therefore, the most likely site of nerve compression is the lateral compartment, affecting the common peroneal nerve.

 

Other Options:

questions.stem: A medical resident is discussing knee joint mechanics with her attending physician. They focus on the process of locking (terminal knee extension) and unlocking (initiating knee flexion), which is crucial for efficient gait. Which muscle is primarily responsible for the unlocking mechanism of the knee joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Popliteus


The popliteus muscle is responsible for the unlocking of the knee joint. Unlocking refers to the initiation of knee flexion, which is critical in starting the process of bending the knee after it has been locked in full extension. 

 

The mnemonic to remember is UP LQ, were 

 

U -Unlocking 

 

P - Popliteus

 

L – Locking 

 

Q – Quadriceps femoris (Vastus medialis)

 

The popliteus acts by rotating the femur laterally on the tibia, allowing the knee to begin flexing.

Options D. Gastrocnemius: The gastrocnemius assists in knee flexion, but it is not primarily responsible for unlocking the knee joint. The unlocking is initiated by the popliteus muscle.

 

Educational objectives:

The sartorius is the longest muscle in the human body (length 45 cm).

The superior boundary of the femoral triangle is formed by the inguinal ligament. The lateral boundary is defined by the sartorius muscle, and the medial boundary is formed by the adductor longus muscle. The apex of the triangle is at the bottom (downside), while the base is at the top (upside). The femoral sheath contains three main structures: the femoral artery, the femoral vein, and the deep inguinal lymph nodes. The femoral nerve is not part of the femoral sheath; it lies outside of the sheath. The femoral sheath has three compartments, with the medial-most compartment containing the femoral canal, where the deep inguinal lymph nodes (Rosenmuller and Cloquet) are located. This arrangement allows for vascular access and is clinically significant for procedures involving the femoral artery or vein.

 

Educational objectives:


The femoral sheath contains the femoral artery, femoral vein, and deep inguinal lymph nodes, but not the femoral nerve, which lies outside the sheath.

The femoral artery is palpable at the groin, specifically at the medial inguinal point. The popliteal artery is palpable at the posterior knee in the popliteal fossa, and the dorsalis pedis artery is palpable at the dorsum of the foot.

 

Educational objectives:


The femoral artery is palpated at the groin, the popliteal artery behind the knee, and the dorsalis pedis artery at the dorsum of the foot.

questions.stem: A group of medical residents is discussing the formation of major nerves of the lower limb. They focus on the sciatic nerve, the largest nerve in the human body. Which of the following options correctly describes the formation of the sciatic nerve?

options.label: A
options.text: Formed by the union of L4-S3 nerve roots

options.label: B
options.text: Formed by the union of L2-L4 nerve roots

options.label: C
options.text: Formed by the union of L5-S2 nerve roots

options.label: D
options.text: Formed by the union of L4-S2 nerve roots

questions.answerText: Formed by the union of L4-S3 nerve roots
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Formed by the union of L4-S3 nerve roots

 

 

The sciatic nerve, the largest and thickest nerve in the human body, is formed by the union of the nerve roots L4, L5, S1, S2, and S3. The nerve has two parts, the common peroneal part and the tibial part, which together form the sciatic nerve. The root values for the sciatic nerve are L4, L5, S1, S2, and S3.

 

Educational objectives:


The sciatic nerve is formed by the union of the nerve roots L4, L5, S1, S2, and S3.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with aching pain and swelling in her left leg, which worsens by the end of the day and improves with leg elevation. Physical examination reveals dilated, tortuous superficial veins in her left medial thigh. Doppler ultrasound confirms venous reflux. Which vein is most likely involved in this patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Great Saphenous Vein


The great saphenous vein is located on the medial side of the leg, and it is the most common vein involved in varicose veins, which are characterized by dilated and tortuous superficial veins, as seen in this patient. The patient's condition improves with leg elevation, which is a classic feature of venous insufficiency or reflux. The femoral vein is a deep vein and is not typically involved in this type of presentation. The popliteal vein is located in the popliteal fossa (behind the knee) and is not associated with medial thigh varicosities. The small saphenous vein is found on the lateral side of the leg, making it unlikely to be involved in this case.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Femoral Vein: This is incorrect because the femoral vein is a deep vein, not a superficial vein, and is not typically involved in varicose veins.

 

Options C. Popliteal Vein: This is incorrect because the popliteal vein is located in the popliteal fossa (behind the knee), not in the medial thigh, and is not commonly associated with varicose veins in this location.

 

Options D. Small Saphenous Vein: This is incorrect because the small saphenous vein is located on the lateral side of the leg, whereas the patient's symptoms are on the medial side, making it unlikely to be involved.

 

Educational objectives:


The great saphenous vein is the most common vein involved in varicose veins, particularly when they are located on the medial side of the thigh.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a complaint of unsteady gait. During examination, when asked to stand on her right leg, her left hip drops. This finding is not observed when she stands on her left leg. This clinical sign indicates weakness in which of the following muscles?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Right Gluteus Medius

 

 

This patient presents with a Trendelenburg sign, which is indicated by the dropping of the opposite side of the pelvis when standing on one leg. When she stands on her right leg and her left hip drops, it suggests that the right gluteus medius muscle is weak. The gluteus medius on the stance side (the side on which the patient is standing) stabilizes the pelvis. In this case, weakness in the right gluteus medius causes the left hip to drop, confirming the involvement of the right gluteus medius.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Left Gluteus Medius: This is incorrect because the left gluteus medius would not cause the left hip to drop when standing on the right leg.

 

Option C. Right Gluteus Maximus: This is incorrect because the gluteus maximus is involved in hip extension, not pelvic stabilization during walking.

 

Option D. Left Gluteus Maximus: This is incorrect because the left gluteus maximus would not affect the pelvis when standing on the right leg, and it is not responsible for stabilizing the pelvis.

 

Educational objectives:
 

A positive Trendelenburg sign, where the opposite hip drops when standing on one leg, indicates weakness in the gluteus medius on the stance leg. In this case, the right gluteus medius is weak.

O opposite pelvis

questions.stem: A 28-year-old professional football player presents with difficulty in kicking a ball. He reports a recent history of decreased strength during knee extension. Additionally, in a separate case, a child with a history of poliomyelitis is observed using his hand to push against his knee to assist in walking. Which muscle group is primarily responsible for knee extension and is likely affected in both cases?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Quadriceps Femoris


The quadriceps femoris is responsible for knee extension. In the case of the football player, decreased strength in knee extension indicates weakness in the quadriceps femoris, which is essential for movements like kicking a ball. Similarly, in the child with poliomyelitis, the hand-knee gait is a classic sign of quadriceps femoris weakness, where the child uses his hand to stabilize the knee during walking due to weakness in this muscle group. The hamstrings are involved in knee flexion, not extension, while the gastrocnemius contributes to plantar flexion, and the tibialis anterior is responsible for foot inversion.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Hamstrings: This is incorrect because the hamstrings are involved in knee flexion, not knee extension.

 

Options B. Gastrocnemius: This is incorrect because the gastrocnemius is involved in plantar flexion of the foot, not knee extension.

 

Options D. Tibialis Anterior: This is incorrect because the tibialis anterior is responsible for foot inversion, not knee extension.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The quadriceps femoris is the primary muscle responsible for knee extension, and its weakness can affect activities like kicking and walking.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a sedentary lifestyle presents with chronic lower extremity edema. On examination, his calf muscles appear underdeveloped. The physician explains the importance of a particular lower limb muscle in venous blood return from the lower extremities. Which muscle is often referred to as the "peripheral heart" due to its role in facilitating venous return?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Soleus


The soleus muscle is often referred to as the "peripheral heart" because its contraction helps pump venous blood back toward the heart. When the soleus contracts, it increases venous return, which in turn increases cardiac output, as venous return is directly proportional to cardiac output. This muscle plays a critical role in aiding circulation, especially in individuals with a sedentary lifestyle where venous return might be impaired.

 

Other Options:
 

Options A. Gastrocnemius: This is incorrect because, although the gastrocnemius is important in calf movements, the soleus is primarily responsible for venous return and is referred to as the "peripheral heart."

 

Options C. Tibialis Anterior: This is incorrect because the tibialis anterior is involved in foot dorsiflexion and does not play a major role in venous return.

 

Options D. Peroneus Longus: This is incorrect because the peroneus longus is involved in foot eversion and does not contribute significantly to venous return.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The soleus muscle is referred to as the "peripheral heart" due to its role in facilitating venous return from the lower extremities.

questions.stem: A patient presented with a sagging face, asymmetrical smile, facial muscle tone with drooping of the left angle of the mouth, eyelid with drooping corners, and inability to blow properly. Which nerve is involved in this case?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Facial nerve


The facial nerve is responsible for supplying all the facial muscles. In this case, the patient presents with facial palsy, which includes signs such as sagging face, asymmetrical smile, drooping of the left angle of the mouth, and inability to blow properly. These signs point to damage or dysfunction of the facial nerve, which controls facial expressions.

 

Other Options:


Options B. Maxillary nerve: This is incorrect because the maxillary nerve provides sensory innervation to the maxillary region and does not supply the facial muscles.

 

Options C. Mandibular nerve: This is incorrect because the mandibular nerve supplies the muscles of mastication and not the muscles responsible for facial expression.

 

Options D. Ophthalmic nerve: This is incorrect because the ophthalmic nerve provides sensory innervation to the ophthalmic area and is not involved in controlling the facial muscles.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Damage to the facial nerve results in facial palsy, affecting facial expressions, including drooping of the face and inability to smile or blow properly.

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of pain in the left side of the neck and noted his tongue pulled to the left side making eating, drinking, and speaking difficult. Two months ago, he had undergone carotid endarterectomy. On examination, the only neurological abnormality noted was the deviation of the tongue as shown in the image, with associated wasting of the left half of the tongue. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Hypoglossal nerve


The hypoglossal nerve (12th cranial nerve) supplies the muscles of the tongue. Damage to the left hypoglossal nerve results in the tongue deviating towards the side of the lesion (in this case, the left side). The tongue muscles are controlled by the hypoglossal nerve, and an injury to this nerve causes the tongue to deviate ipsilaterally (towards the injured side). The associated wasting of the left half of the tongue further confirms the involvement of the left hypoglossal nerve.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Lingual nerve: This is incorrect because the lingual nerve is responsible for sensory innervation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and is not responsible for tongue movements.

 

Options B. Facial nerve: This is incorrect because the facial nerve is responsible for facial muscles and is not involved in the movement of the tongue.

 

Options D. Vagus nerve: This is incorrect because the vagus nerve (10th cranial nerve) does not supply the muscles of the tongue.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Damage to the hypoglossal nerve results in tongue deviation towards the affected side and is responsible for controlling the muscles of the tongue.

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male sustained a head injury due to a fall from his bike. CT brain showed features as shown in the image. The blood vessel injury is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Middle meningeal artery


The CT scan shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) opacity, which is a classic feature of an epidural hemorrhage (EDH). EDH occurs when blood collects between the dura mater and the skull, often as a result of trauma, such as fractures in the temporal or parietal bone. Symptoms typically have a rapid onset and may include headache, vomiting, and altered consciousness, sometimes with a lucid interval. This type of hemorrhage is commonly associated with damage to the middle meningeal artery, which is located between the dura mater and the skull.

 

Other Options:


 

Option A) Middle cerebral artery: This is incorrect. The middle cerebral artery is typically involved in other forms of brain injury, such as ischemic or hemorrhagic strokes, not in epidural hemorrhage.

 

Option B) Superior cerebral vein: This is incorrect. The superior cerebral vein is typically involved in subdural hemorrhage, where blood collects between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.

 

Option D) Accessory meningeal artery: This is incorrect. The middle meningeal artery is the most commonly injured vessel in cases of epidural hemorrhage, not the accessory meningeal artery.

 

Educational objectives:
 

A biconvex (lens-shaped) opacity on CT scan after head trauma indicates an epidural hemorrhage (EDH), most commonly caused by injury to the middle meningeal artery.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man underwent parotidectomy, following which he complained that there was loss of sensation while shaving. Which nerve is most likely affected?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Greater auricular nerve


The greater auricular nerve supplies sensation to the angle of the mandible, which is the area involved in this case. The patient complains of loss of sensation in the shaving area, specifically around the angle of the mandible, following the parotidectomy. The greater auricular nerve is responsible for the sensory innervation of this region.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Auriculotemporal nerve: This is incorrect because the auriculotemporal nerve supplies the auricle and temporal region, not the angle of the mandible.

 

Options C. Mandibular nerve: This is incorrect because the mandibular nerve supplies the muscles of mastication and does not provide sensory innervation to the angle of the mandible.

 

Options D. Facial nerve: This is incorrect because the facial nerve supplies the muscles of the face and is not involved in sensory innervation of the angle of the mandible.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The greater auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the angle of the mandible, and its damage during a parotidectomy can lead to loss of sensation in this area.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with painful vesicular eruptions as shown in the image. Which division of the trigeminal nerve is involved?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) V1


The painful vesicular eruptions are located near the eye, along the dermatome of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve. This division of the trigeminal nerve includes branches such as the supratrochlear, supraorbital, lacrimal, infratrochlear, and external nasal nerve, which supply sensation to the area around the forehead and the eye.

 

Other Options:


Options B. V2: This is incorrect because the maxillary division (V2) supplies the maxilla region, not the area near the eye.

 

Options C. V3: This is incorrect because the mandibular division (V3) supplies the mandibular area, not the area near the eye.

 

Options D. V4: This option does not exist.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve supplies the skin near the eye, and involvement of this division can lead to painful vesicular eruptions in that area.

options.label: A
options.text: It is located on the dorsal aspect of hand and becomes visible when the thumb is fully abducted and adducted

options.label: B
options.text: Floor is formed by styloid process of radius, base of first metacarpal bone

options.label: C
options.text: Medially by tendon of extensor pollicis brevis

options.label: D
options.text: Laterally by extensor carpi radialis longus

questions.answerText: Floor is formed by styloid process of radius, base of first metacarpal bone
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Floor is formed by styloid process of radius, base of first metacarpal bone

 

 

The highlighted area in the image represents the anatomical snuff box, which is bounded by the abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, and extensor pollicis longus tendons. The floor of the anatomical snuff box is formed by the styloid process of the radius, the scaphoid, the trapezium, and the base of the first metacarpal bone.

 

Other Options:


Options A. It is located on the dorsal aspect of hand and becomes visible when the thumb is fully abducted and adducted: This is incorrect because the anatomical snuff box becomes visible when the thumb is fully extended, not when it is abducted or adducted.

 

Options C. Medially by tendon of extensor pollicis brevis: This is incorrect because the extensor pollicis brevis forms part of the lateral boundary, not the medial boundary.

 

Options D. Laterally by extensor carpi radialis longus: This is incorrect because the extensor carpi radialis longus is not involved in forming the lateral boundary of the anatomical snuff box.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The floor of the anatomical snuff box is formed by the styloid process of the radius, the scaphoid, the trapezium, and the base of the first metacarpal bone.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman whose impacted left lower wisdom tooth was surgically removed. The operation lasted about an hour, and the dental surgeon suspected that some nerves might have been bruised during the operation. The patient presented with loss of sensation in the gums of her lower jaw, and her mouth was slightly dry. On examination, the general sensation in the tongue was diminished in the anterior two-thirds, but it was normal in the posterior portion. Which among the following nerves has been injured in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Lingual nerve


The lingual nerve is responsible for the sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and gums of the lower jaw. The loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the loss of sensation in the gums of the lower jaw suggest damage to the lingual nerve. Although the taste sensation is mediated by the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (VII), which is the best answer, but as not given in the options, so the next best answer is  lingual nerve. 

 

Other Options:


Options A. Hypoglossal nerve: This is incorrect because the hypoglossal nerve supplies motor innervation to the muscles of the tongue and does not affect sensation or taste.

 

Options B. Glossopharyngeal nerve: This is incorrect because the glossopharyngeal nerve is responsible for taste and sensation in the posterior one-third of the tongue, not the anterior two-thirds.

 

Options D. Vagus nerve: This is incorrect because the vagus nerve is not involved in sensation or taste in the anterior part of the tongue.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The lingual nerve supplies sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and gums of the lower jaw. Damage to the lingual nerve during dental surgery can result in loss of sensation and diminished taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old male rock climber spent the day climbing outdoors with a partner. They hiked to the base of the climb carrying their gear in backpacks. After a day of climbing, they hurried to return to their vehicle because of the imminent loss of daylight. He carried his climbing gear slung over his shoulder. As he was approaching the trailhead, he noted some soreness in his right neck area. After hiking 4 hours back to his vehicle, while carrying approximately 20 pounds of gear in this manner, he realized he was unable to shrug his right shoulder. He reports being incapable of contracting his trapezius or being able to fully elevate the affected arm for 3 days. As there was no improvement, he sought medical advice. Which of the following nerves has been injured in the above scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Spinal accessory nerve


The patient is unable to contract the trapezius muscle, which indicates damage to the spinal accessory nerve. The spinal accessory nerve is responsible for innervating the trapezius muscle. This nerve is the most likely to be affected given the history of carrying gear slung over the shoulder for an extended period, leading to nerve compression or injury.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Axillary nerve
This is incorrect because the axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor muscles, not the trapezius.

 

Options C. Thoracodorsal nerve
This is incorrect because the thoracodorsal nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi, not the trapezius.

 

Options D. Dorsal scapular nerve
This is incorrect because the dorsal scapular nerve supplies the levator scapulae, rhomboid major, and rhomboid minor, not the trapezius.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The spinal accessory nerve innervates the trapezius muscle, and its injury can result in the inability to shrug the shoulder or elevate the arm.

questions.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man as shown in the image presents with weakness in his hand. He reports difficulty extending his wrist and fingers and a decreased sensation on the back of his hand. These symptoms have progressively worsened over the past few weeks. Which of the following structures is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Posterior cord


The patient presents with wrist drop, which indicates damage to the radial nerve. The radial nerve is responsible for wrist and finger extension as well as sensation on the back of the hand. In this case, the posterior cord of the brachial plexus is most likely affected, as it gives rise to the radial nerve. The condition described is an example of crutch palsy, where prolonged pressure in the axilla (from crutches or heavy loads) can compress the posterior cord.

 

Other Options:


Options B. Lateral cord: This is incorrect because the lateral cord contributes to the formation of the median nerve, not the radial nerve.

 

Options C. Medial cord: This is incorrect because the medial cord forms the ulnar nerve, not the radial nerve.

 

Options D. Upper trunk: This is incorrect because the upper trunk is located in the neck and not involved in this case of axillary compression.

 

Educational objectives:
 

In cases of wrist drop and decreased sensation on the back of the hand, damage to the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, which gives rise to the radial nerve, is the most likely cause.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old office worker complains of persistent wrist pain and difficulty performing repetitive tasks on a computer keyboard. Physical examination reveals tenderness at the wrist joint and decreased range of motion, particularly during wrist flexion and extension. Radiographic evaluation shows evidence of degenerative changes in the joint space. Which of the following bones is not directly involved in the formation of the wrist joint?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ulna


The wrist joint is primarily the radiocarpal joint, which involves the radius and carpal bones like the scaphoid and triquetral. The ulna does not directly participate in the formation of the wrist joint because it is separated from the wrist joint by a thin plate of cartilage. This is why the radiocarpal joint does not include the ulna.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Scaphoid: This is incorrect because the scaphoid is a carpal bone that directly participates in the radiocarpal joint.

 

Options C. Radius: This is incorrect because the radius is one of the main bones involved in the formation of the radiocarpal joint.

 

Options D. Triquetral: This is incorrect because the triquetral is a carpal bone that also participates in the radiocarpal joint.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The ulna does not participate in the wrist (radiocarpal) joint, whereas the radius and carpal bones like the scaphoid and triquetral.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old patient with a history of hypertension and diabetes is admitted to the hospital with complaints of weakness in the hand and difficulty holding objects. The patient's medical history includes a recent cerebrovascular accident (CVA). A "test" is performed as shown in the image as part of the neurological examination. Which of the following muscle groups is primarily assessed with this test to check for motor function in the hand?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Palmar interossei


The CARD test shown in the image assesses the function of the palmar interossei muscles. These muscles are responsible for adduction of the fingers and are supplied by the ulnar nerve. The patient is asked to hold the card between the fingers, and failure to hold the card indicates weakness in the palmar interossei.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Lumbricals:
This is incorrect because the lumbricals are involved in the flexion of the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension of the interphalangeal joints, but they are not primarily assessed in this test.

 

Options C. Dorsal interossei:
This is incorrect because the dorsal interossei muscles are responsible for abduction of the fingers, and they are tested with the IGAWA test, not the CARD test.

 

Options D. Adductor pollicis:
This is incorrect because the adductor pollicis is tested using the book test, not the CARD test.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The palmar interossei muscles, responsible for adduction of the fingers, are assessed by the CARD test, which checks for ulnar nerve function.

questions.stemHtml: The marked structure contains:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Elastin cartilage


The marked structure in the image refers to the epiglottis, which is made of elastin cartilage. The epiglottis is an important structure that prevents food from entering the airway during swallowing. The elastin cartilage is one of the key types of cartilage in the human body.

 

Nearby structures:

 

Nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx are the three parts of the pharynx, each connected to specific anatomical landmarks, such as the nasal cavity, oral cavity, and esophagus. The epiglottis itself is located in the laryngopharynx, where it plays a crucial role in protecting the airway.

 

To help differentiate between cartilage types, a mnemonic can be used:

 

Hyaline cartilage is found in:

 

  • G: Growth plates
    • F: Fetal cartilage
    • C: Costal cartilages (costochondral junctions)
    • A: Articular surfaces of bones
    • R: Respiratory tract (C-shaped cartilage of the trachea)

 

Elastin cartilage is found in 3E locations:

 

  • Epiglottis
    • Ear pinna

    • Eustachian tube

       

Fibrocartilage is represented by the FIAT Logo mnemonic:

 

  • F: Fibrocartilage
    • I: Intervertebral discs
    • A: Articular discs (e.g., temporomandibular joint)
    • T: Tendon insertions
    • L: Labrum (e.g., glenoid labrum)

 

Other Options:


 

Options A. Hyaline cartilage: This is incorrect because hyaline cartilage is primarily found in growth plates, articular surfaces, and the respiratory tract, not in the epiglottis.

 

Options C. Fibrocartilage: This is incorrect because fibrocartilage is found in structures like intervertebral discs, glenoid labrum, and articular discs, not in the epiglottis.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The epiglottis is composed of elastin cartilage, which is crucial for its function during swallowing. The 3E mnemonic (Epiglottis, Ear pinna, Eustachian tube) helps remember structures made of elastin cartilage.

questions.stemHtml: Which nerve is thickened in the following image of a patient with Hansen's disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Great auricular nerve


In the case of Hansen’s disease (leprosy), several nerves can become thickened, but the great auricular nerve is a common site of involvement, especially in the neck region. The great auricular nerve runs behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle, as seen in the image, and splits into an anterior division that supplies the angle of the mandible, and a posterior division that supplies the pinna of the ear.

 

This nerve is particularly important in Hansen’s disease, as it is prone to thickening. The most commonly involved nerves in leprosy are the ulnar nerve, common peroneal nerve, and the great auricular nerve in the neck, which is the case here.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Supraclavicular nerves: These nerves are located above the clavicle and are divided into medial, intermediate, and lateral branches. They are not typically involved in Hansen’s disease and do not match the location of the thickened nerve in the image.

 

Options B. Dorsal scapular nerve: This nerve supplies the levator scapulae, rhomboid major, and rhomboid minor muscles. It is found on the dorsal (back) side of the body and is not located in the area shown in the image.

 

Options D. Transverse cervical cutaneous nerve: This nerve runs transversely across the neck, supplying the skin of the anterior neck region. It is not located in the same position as the thickened nerve seen in the image and does not run towards the auricle, unlike the great auricular nerve.

In Hansen’s disease (leprosy), the great auricular nerve is commonly thickened, particularly in the neck, running behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle and supplying the angle of the mandible and the pinna.

questions.stemHtml: Injury of which of the following nerves causes drooping of the shoulder?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B


Drooping of the shoulder is caused by paralysis of the trapezius muscle, which is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI). The trapezius muscle originates from the external occipital protuberance and inserts into the lateral third of the clavicle. The spinal root of the accessory nerve (nerve B in the image) is responsible for innervating this muscle, and damage to this nerve leads to weakness or paralysis of the trapezius, causing the characteristic drooping of the shoulder.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Lesser occipital nerve: This nerve supplies the skin of the posterior scalp and has no role in innervating the trapezius muscle or affecting shoulder movement. It is not responsible for shoulder drooping.

 

Options C. Mastoid process: The mastoid process is a bony landmark on the temporal bone and does not innervate any muscles or have a role in shoulder movement.

 

Options D. Transverse cutaneous nerve of the neck: This nerve supplies the skin of the anterior and lateral neck. It is unrelated to the innervation of the trapezius muscle and does not contribute to shoulder movement.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Injury to the spinal accessory nerve, which innervates the trapezius muscle, leads to shoulder drooping. The nerve responsible is identified as B in the image.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the nerve passing through Dorello’s canal:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) C

 

The nerve passing through Dorello’s canal is the 6th cranial nerve (abducens nerve). Dorello’s canal is a dural canal located near the apex of the petrous part of the temporal bone, and the 6th cranial nerve passes through this canal as it exits the brainstem. The abducens nerve is responsible for innervating the lateral rectus muscle of the eye, which controls the movement of the eyeball.

 

In the image, C represents the 6th cranial nerve, running through Dorello’s canal near the cavernous sinus, along with other important neurovascular structures.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. 3rd cranial nerve (oculomotor nerve): This nerve is involved in controlling most of the eye movements and is located in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus but does not pass through Dorello’s canal.

 

Options B. 4th cranial nerve (trochlear nerve): This nerve controls the superior oblique muscle of the eye and is also located in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus but does not pass through Dorello’s canal.

 

Options D. V1 (ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve): This division of the trigeminal nerve provides sensory innervation to the forehead, scalp, and upper eyelid, and passes through the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, not Dorello’s canal.

 

Educational objectives:

 

The 6th cranial nerve (abducens nerve) passes through Dorello’s canal and is closely associated with the cavernous sinus.

questions.stem: Which of the following structure, when bilaterally ablated, leads to an inability to form long-term memories?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hippocampus


The hippocampus is responsible for converting short-term memory into long-term memory. If there is damage to the hippocampus, there is an inability to form new long-term memories, leading to memory loss.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A.  Amygdala: This almond-shaped structure is involved in emotional responses, particularly fear and pleasure, as well as behaviors like food intake and sexual activity. It does not directly control memory formation.

 

Options C.  Cingulate gyrus: This region is part of the limbic system and is associated with emotional regulation and satisfaction but is not primarily responsible for memory consolidation.

 

Options D. Dorsomedial nucleus of thalamus: The thalamus acts as a relay station for sensory signals, sending information to different parts of the brain. It is not primarily involved in memory processing.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The hippocampus is essential for the consolidation of short-term memories into long-term memories. Damage to this structure impairs the ability to form new long-term memories, a condition known as anterograde amnesia.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the type of fibre marked in the given diagram:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Projection fibres


The structure indicated by the arrow is the internal capsule, a boomerang-shaped bundle of projection fibres. Projection fibres connect the cerebral cortex to lower areas of the brain and spinal cord, transmitting motor commands and sensory information.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Long association fibres: These connect distant areas within the same hemisphere of the brain but are not involved here.
 

Options B. Short association fibres: These connect adjacent gyri within the same hemisphere, not relevant to the internal capsule.
 

Options D.  Commissural fibres: These connect corresponding areas between the two hemispheres, such as the corpus callosum, but are not indicated in this case.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The internal capsule is made up of projection fibres that transmit signals between the cortex and lower brain structures.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is not a likely consequence of occlusion of the artery supplying the indicated area?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Astereognosis


The marked area in the image represents the paracentral lobule, which is involved in controlling motor and sensory functions related to the perineal region, including the urinary bladder, anal canal, and genitals. Occlusion of the artery supplying this area, typically the anterior cerebral artery, can lead to urinary incontinence, rectal incontinence, and perianal anesthesia. However, astereognosis (the inability to recognize objects by touch) is not related to this area; it is usually associated with damage to the parietal lobe, particularly the sensory pathways, such as the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus.

 

Other Options:

 

Options A. Urinary incontinence: The paracentral lobule controls bladder function, so incontinence is a likely consequence.
 

Options B. Rectal incontinence: The paracentral lobule also controls bowel function, so rectal incontinence is a likely result of damage.
 

Options D. Perianal anaesthesia: Loss of sensation in the perineal region is likely due to damage in this area.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Damage to the paracentral lobule causes incontinence and sensory deficits in the perineal region but does not result in astereognosis, which is linked to damage in sensory processing areas of the parietal lobe.

questions.stemHtml: Which area of the cerebrum, if affected, would result in a patient knowing what they want to speak but being unable to do so?
questions.solutionHtml:
A) B)


Damage to Broca's area (located in area 44 and 45 of the brain) can lead to Broca's aphasia, where a patient knows what they want to say but is unable to speak properly. Broca's aphasia is characterized by difficulties in speech production, though the ability to understand language remains intact. Broca's area is essential for the motor control of speech, and a lesion here impairs the brain's ability to produce coherent speech, although the patient's cognitive functions related to understanding language remain unaffected.

 

Other Options:
 

Options A. This area corresponds to the prefrontal lobe, which is involved in judgment, behavior, personality, and higher cognitive skills, but it is not related to speech production.
 

Options C. This is the primary auditory area, which is related to hearing and not directly involved in speech production.
 

Options D.This is the occipital lobe, which is responsible for vision and has no role in speech or language processing.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Damage to Broca's area (area 44 and 45) results in Broca's aphasia, where the patient can comprehend language but is unable to produce speech effectively.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is incorrectly marked?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypothalamus


D is incorrectly marked as the hypothalamus. The label "D" in the image is pointing to the pituitary, not the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is located above and slightly anterior to the pituitary gland. The pituitary is an important gland responsible for hormone regulation, but it is not part of the hypothalamus.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Genu of corpus callosum: This is correctly marked. The genu is the front part of the corpus callosum, the structure that connects the two cerebral hemispheres.
 

Options B. Columns of fornix: This is correctly marked. The fornix is a part of the brain involved in memory formation, and its columns are accurately labeled.
 

Options C. Cerebellum: This is also correctly marked. The cerebellum is responsible for motor coordination and is located at the back of the brain.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The pituitary gland is often confused with the hypothalamus due to their proximity, but they are distinct structures with different functions.

questions.stemHtml: The marked cells inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei. Identify the cell:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Purkinje cell


The marked cell is a Purkinje cell, which is located in the Purkinje layer of the cerebellum. Purkinje cells are the only efferent cells in the cerebellar cortex and are known for their inhibitory function on the deep cerebellar nuclei. These cells release inhibitory neurotransmitters, such as GABA, which suppress the activity of the deep cerebellar nuclei, thereby regulating motor coordination.

 

Other Options:


Options A. Golgi cell: Found in the granular layer, Golgi cells are involved in modulating the activity of granule cells but do not inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei.


Options B. Basket cell: These cells are found in the molecular layer and provide inhibitory input to Purkinje cells, not the deep cerebellar nuclei.
 

Options D. Granular cell: These excitatory cells are located in the granular layer and do not inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei.

 

Educational objectives:

 

5 neurons of cerebellum:- (BSP GoGa)

  • S - Stellate cells
  • P - Purkinje cells :- largest, only efferent fibers present, inhibitory to deep cerebellar nuclei.
  • Go - Golgi cells
  • Ga (sir):- Granular

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following speech disorders is caused by the injury of the structure shown in the histology image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dysarthria


The cerebellum, as shown in the histological image, is responsible for muscle coordination, balance, and fine motor control. Injury to the cerebellum leads to dysarthria, a motor speech disorder that affects the muscles used for speaking, resulting in slurred or slow speech. Dysarthria is a common symptom of cerebellar damage, as the cerebellum plays a key role in coordinating the movements required for proper articulation.

 

Other Options:
 

Options A. Apraxia: This is a motor planning disorder that affects the ability to carry out voluntary movements, but it is not directly related to cerebellar injury.
 

Options B. Aphasia: This refers to a loss of ability to understand or express speech, typically due to damage to language centers like Broca's or Wernicke's areas, not the cerebellum.
 

Options D. Dysprosody: This is a disorder of speech melody or intonation and is not directly associated with cerebellar injury.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Injury to the cerebellum can cause dysarthria, a speech disorder characterized by impaired articulation due to a lack of muscle coordination.

questions.stemHtml: In the following image, deficient synthesis of neurotransmitter may lead to Parkinson's disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B


The area labeled B is the Substantia Nigra, located in the midbrain. It is responsible for the synthesis of dopamine, a key neurotransmitter involved in movement control. In Parkinson's disease, the neurons in the Substantia Nigra degenerate, leading to a deficiency in dopamine production, which causes the characteristic motor symptoms of the disease, such as tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia.

 

Other Options:


Options A. This is the caudate nucleus, involved in motor control but not directly linked to dopamine synthesis in Parkinson's disease.
 

Options C. This area is likely part of the pons, which has no direct connection to Parkinson's disease or dopamine synthesis.
 

Options D. This area points to the medulla oblongata, which is involved in autonomic functions, not the synthesis of dopamine.

 

Educational objectives:
 

Degeneration of the Substantia Nigra results in a dopamine deficit, which is the primary cause of the motor symptoms seen in Parkinson's disease.

questions.stemHtml: Superior, inferior & facial colliculus are indicated respectively as?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) B, C, D


The superior colliculus, inferior colliculus, and facial colliculus are all located in the brainstem. These structures are vital for various sensory and motor functions.

 

B indicates the superior colliculus, which is involved in visual reflexes and coordinating head and eye movements.

 

C indicates the inferior colliculus, which plays an essential role in auditory processing and reflexive responses to sounds.

 

D indicates the facial colliculus, which is formed by the fibers of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) as they loop around the abducens nucleus in the floor of the fourth ventricle.

 

Educational objectives:
 

The superior colliculus (B), inferior colliculus (C), and facial colliculus (D) are three important structures located on the dorsal surface of the brainstem. The superior and inferior colliculi are part of the midbrain's tectum, while the facial colliculus is found in the pons, forming the facial nerve's nucleus projection.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the vertebra?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) C2
 

The vertebra shown in the image is C2, also known as the axis. A defining feature of C2 is the odontoid process (or dens), which is visible in the image. The dens projects upward and serves as a pivotal point for the rotation of the C1 vertebra (the atlas) around the axis, allowing for head rotation. Other Options:
